scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Mek Mulung developed in the village of Wang Tepus in Kedah, Malaysia, establishing strong community roots by the late 18th century.
It absorbed narrative, dance, and theatrical devices from regional styles including Mak Yong, Menora, and Hadrah.
Originally possessing a repertoire of approximately twenty legendary stories, only a small number of these plays continue to be enacted.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Traditionally staged as an act of celebration and thanksgiving following a bountiful agricultural harvest, a complete Mek Mulung performance can extend across three nights.
The event commences on the preceding day with a communal feast for performers, neighbors, and visitors, serving as a pillar of village fellowship and social communication.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performances begin with the Bertabuh instrumental opening, followed by Bertabik, an opening choral song accompanied by synchronized dance movement.
The physical vocabulary focuses on the upper body, featuring rapid, abbreviated arm swings that oscillate forward, backward, up, and down.

Up to seven specific dances are staged across the production: Tarian Sembah, Tarian Gambang, Tarian Puteri Mabuk, Tarian Anak Menora, Tarian Sirama, Tarian Puteri Masuk Bilik Air, and Tarian Sedayung.
Watch for To-and-fro arm swing, Up-and-down arm swing.

Formation: Staged centrally within an open barn with spectators enclosing the playing space.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The musical accompaniment is predominantly percussive and driven by an orchestra of rebana drums, gongs, and kecerek (metal or wooden concussion sticks).
A single small oboe provides the only melodic instrumental voice.
Listen for the rebana, gong, kecerek, small oboe.

A sharp, clattering percussive foundation dominated by the rhythmic snapping of kecerek concussion sticks and resonance of rebana drums, underscored by deep gong strokes. Piercing above this percussive wall is the reedy, sustained contour of a single small oboe, accompanied by unornamented syllabic group singing.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Mek Mulung is performed in an open barn environment where the audience surrounds the acting troupe of fifteen to twenty people.
Lead characters such as the king and princess wear traditional Malay royal attire.
In historical practice, male performers wore women's dress to embody female roles; modern productions feature both male and female performers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Pak Mulung serves as the central reciter of Hikayat texts within the performance structure.
Historical productions were sustained exclusively by male actors and musicians who passed the oral repertoire directly down family lines.
The art form is native specifically to Kedah in northwest Malaysia, with historical roots centered in the village of Wang Tepus.

Historically preserved through oral transmission from elder village practitioners to their offspring, the lineage has expanded into modern institutional instruction, including academic seminars, primary and secondary school programs, university forums, and cultural preservation festivals.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Mek Mulung is influence of Mak Yong: Shares dramatic narrative structure, royalty character archetypes, and combined song, dance, and dialogue elements.
Mek Mulung is influence of Menora: Contributed performance conventions and stylistic components to northwestern Malay folk theatre.
Mek Mulung is influence of Hadrah: Influenced vocal and percussive performance practices in northern Malay theatrical traditions.
